title: The Investiture of the Gods
subtitle: King Wu's Campaign Against Zhou · The Gods' Investiture Rolls Under Three Teachings
description: The Investiture of the Gods is a full-length fantasy novel of gods and demons by the Ming-dynasty writer Xu Zhonglin (or, by some accounts, Lu Xixing), comprising one hundred chapters. Built on the historical framework of King Wu's campaign against King Zhou and the transition from Shang to Zhou, with the flesh and blood of the Taoist immortal battles between the Chan and Jie teachings, it creates such household mythic figures as Jiang Ziya, Nezha, Yang Jian, and Daji. The titles of the three hundred and sixty-five principal deities on the Investiture Rolls have long been woven into the bloodstream of Chinese folk belief.

route.title: The Investiture of the Gods: The Dark Bird of Heaven's Mandate — A Mythic Journey to the Birth of Shang
route.intro:
When Heaven is about to entrust a great mission, it first steels a man's will. The famous names on the Investiture Rolls roam freely across the Three Realms and Five Elements.
Xu Zhonglin (c. 1567–1620), literary name Old Hermit of Mount Zhong, was a native of Yingtian Prefecture (modern Nanjing). He lived in the mid-to-late Ming dynasty, when the fusion of Buddhism, Taoism, and Confucianism provided fertile soil for the creation of The Investiture of the Gods. The novel fuses the history of the Shang–Zhou dynastic transition with the imagination of immortals battling with magic powers, producing both a sweeping epic and a dazzling portrait gallery of gods and demons. Let us follow the Road of Investiture — from the Stag Terrace of Zhaoge to the Zhou Plains of Western Qi, from the banks of the Wei River where Jiang the Grand Duke fished to the Investiture Terrace itself — visiting the national heritage sites that bear witness to the great god-demon wars and the succession of dynasties.

stops.title: Stop One: Zhaoge · Three Thousand Years of the Stag Terrace at Yinxu
stops.content: King Zhou of Shang built the Stag Terrace at Zhaoge, "a thousand feet high, reaching to the clouds and rain," where he feasted and reveled with Daji day and night. Bi Gan's heart being ripped out, the burning pillar of the Paoluo punishment, the pools of wine and forests of meat — the luxury and cruelty of Zhaoge laid the inevitable groundwork for King Wu's campaign. And mythic tales like Nezha stirring up the sea and Leizhenzi's birth began to spread from this doomed capital. The Yinxu Ruins in Anyang are precisely the late Shang capital. Here oracle bone script was discovered, and China's documented history begins. Along the banks of the Huan River, the foundations of palace and ancestral temple buildings and sacrificial pits are still clearly visible. Standing on Yinxu's ground, every inch of soil beneath your feet is steeped in three-thousand-year-old memories — the cold gleam of bronze, the mysterious incised lines on oracle bones — making you feel as if you can hear the last bells of Zhaoge city. The Stag Terrace is long gone, but the discovery of Yinxu brought that distant dynasty back to life. Yinxu straddles the north and south banks of the Huan River, covering a total area of about thirty-six square kilometers. Since excavation began in 1928, tens of thousands of oracle bone fragments and thousands of bronze vessels have been unearthed, along with the world-shocking Tomb of Fu Hao at Yinxu — the only intact Shang royal tomb. Fu Hao was both queen of King Wu Ding and a female general. The over four hundred bronze vessels, more than seven hundred jade objects, and over six thousand cowrie shells found in her tomb silently speak of that era's incredible richness. Standing on the earthen platform of the palace-ancestral temple zone, you look out across the wilderness — the autumn wind stirs the reeds along the Huan River. Three thousand years ago, the aroma of sacrificial meat wafted from the bronze cauldrons, the crackle of oracle bones splitting in flames seems still to echo faintly on the wind. Walking through Yinxu, you cannot miss the sacrificial pits in the ancestral temple area — rows of orderly human sacrifice pits and chariot pits both terrify and convey a primitive, brutal solemnity. The narrative of "King Zhou lost the Way, the realm turned from him" in The Investiture of the Gods becomes strikingly real before these sacrificial pits. When Jiang Ziya in the novel recites the Investiture Rolls, he intones: "By the decree of the Primordial Heavenly Worthy, Lord of Primordial Beginning..." Behind this decree lie countless bodies that were sacrificed and offered up. Every oracle bone at Yinxu bears the three characters "王占曰" (The king divined and said). The Shang king consulted the spirits through divination and decided state policy — the worldview of Investiture of the Gods originates precisely here: the interweaving of the three realms of man, spirit, and ghost, the unceasing flux of Heaven's mandate. Crossing to the royal cemetery on the north bank of the Huan River, the massive tomb pits are over ten meters deep, their ramps slanting into the earth like wounds in the land. The Simuwu Ding was unearthed here — an 832-kilogram bronze giant cauldron, four-legged and square-bodied, its taotie mask design fearsome and ferocious. Gazing down into the deep, dark pit, it seems as if the black hole might suck you into the darkness of three thousand years ago. And the immortals of the Jie teaching, who turned to ash in the Immortals-Slaying Formation and the Ten Thousand Immortals Formation of The Investiture of the Gods — were they not likewise devoured by a greater order called "Heaven's Mandate"? The bells of Zhaoge city have fallen silent, but the wind at Yinxu still blows — across the palace foundations, across the oracle bone fragments, across the bones and blood of a dynasty.

stops.title: Stop Two: The Zhou Plains of Western Qi · The Phoenix Sings at Qishan
stops.content: King Wen of Zhou, Ji Chang, was imprisoned by King Zhou at Youli for seven years, where he expanded the Eight Trigrams into the Sixty-Four Hexagrams. After returning to his state, he practiced benevolent governance in Western Qi, recruiting worthy talents — "the phoenix sings, on that high ridge" — the Zhou people gathered strength in the Wei River valley, awaiting the descent of Heaven's mandate. When King Wu succeeded the throne, he made Jiang Ziya his military counselor, assembled the eight hundred lords at Mengjin, and marched in full force toward Zhaoge. The Zhou Plains Site in the Fufeng and Qishan area of Baoji is precisely the birthplace of the Zhou people. Here large palace and ancestral temple foundations and bronze hoards have been discovered, yielding such national treasures as the Mao Gong Ding and the Da Ke Ding, earning the area the name "Home of Bronze Vessels." And the Duke of Zhou Temple at the southern foot of Phoenix Mountain in Qishan is the shrine dedicated to the Duke of Zhou, Ji Dan, who laid the foundation for the Zhou dynasty's eight-hundred-year rule — creating rites and music that made "ritual" the soul of Chinese civilization. From the Zhou Plains to the Duke of Zhou Temple, the legend of the phoenix singing at Qishan has never faded. Entering the core area of the Zhou Plains Site — the courtyard building foundation of the Fengchu Group — a three-thousand-year-old "courtyard house" is laid out before your eyes. The screen wall, gate, front hall, rear chamber, east and west wing rooms are all distinguishable, and even the drainage pottery pipes are well preserved. This building complex covers nearly 1,500 square meters — the earliest and most complete courtyard-style palace building yet discovered in China. In the Book of Songs, Great Elegance, the line "The Duke of Tanfu, came at dawn spurring his horse, following the western riverbank until he reached the foot of Mount Qi" — it was because the Duke of Tanfu led the Zhou people from Bin to the foot of Mount Qi that the auspicious sign of "the phoenix sings at Qishan" could later appear. Standing on the palace foundation, you can still discern where the courtyard was located three thousand years ago — perhaps King Wen paced here, working out the sixty-four hexagrams, awaiting the descent of Heaven's mandate. A drive of less than an hour from the Zhou Plains brings you to the Duke of Zhou Temple. First built in the Tang dynasty, this temple is built against Phoenix Mountain in three ascending courtyards. In the main hall, the statue of the Duke of Zhou, Ji Dan, sits upright in the center — his robes loose and wide, his countenance gentle. The Duke assisted the young King Cheng in pacifying the Rebellion of the Three Guardians, created rites and music, and laid the institutional foundation for the Zhou dynasty's eight hundred years. Though The Investiture of the Gods does not directly portray the Duke of Zhou, in Jiang Ziya's story of assisting King Wu, overthrowing Zhou, and investing the gods, the Duke's shadow is everywhere — Jiang Ziya handled military affairs, the Duke of Zhou handled institutions — one civil, one martial — together propping up the Zhou dynasty. The ancient cypresses in the temple are gnarled and vigorous, some over a thousand years old, their twisted branches reaching toward the sky like the Duke of Zhou's hands, still tracing the outline of rites and music for Chinese civilization across the ages. Leaving the Duke of Zhou Temple and looking back at Mount Qi — this is the Qishan of "the phoenix sings at Qishan." The mountain is not tall but graceful, its twin peaks facing each other like paired watchtowers opening in the sky. The Discourses of the State records: "When Zhou was rising, the yuanchuo sang on Mount Qi." The yuanchuo is the phoenix — the Zhou people concretized Heaven's mandate as a divine bird, using its call to announce the arrival of a new era. As the sun sets, the ochre-red sandstone of Mount Qi glows in the twilight like burning flames. The sound of the phoenix's song has long faded, but the gene of "ritual" has been carved into the blood of every Chinese person. From the Zhou Plains to the Duke of Zhou Temple, the road is short — short enough to walk in half a day. And it is also very long — so long that after walking it for over three thousand years, we have still not reached its end.

stops.title: Stop Three: The Investiture Terrace · All Gods Take Their Places at the Taihao Mausoleum
stops.content: At the Battle of Muye, the Shang army turned their weapons around. King Zhou burned himself to death on the Stag Terrace. Jiang Ziya ascended the terrace to invest the gods, and the three hundred and sixty-five principal deities each took their appointed place — loyal ministers and good generals who died in battle, immortals of the Jie teaching who fell, and even King Zhou and Daji found their names on the Investiture Rolls. From that day forward, the words "Investiture of the Gods" entered the collective memory of the Chinese people. Gods and demons were no longer remote beings aloof from the world, but creatures of feeling and righteousness, joy and sorrow — just like us. The Taihao Mausoleum and Temple in Huaiyang, Zhoukou, is the vast mausoleum and temple complex dedicated to the human progenitor Taihao Fuxi, known as "the foremost mausoleum under heaven." Fuxi is more ancient than the gods of the Investiture Rolls — he drew the Eight Trigrams, wove nets, established marriage rites, and inaugurated the dawn of Chinese civilization. The story of the Investiture of the Gods closes a meaningful circle here: the destination where all gods return to their places is also the starting point of the human progenitor. Every second day of the second lunar month, the Taihao Mausoleum temple fair draws massive crowds — three thousand years of mythic stories eventually merge into the simplest incense offerings of the mortal world. The Taihao Mausoleum and Temple covers over eight hundred mu, divided into an outer city, inner city, and forbidden city. Entering through the Meridian Gate and proceeding north along the central axis, you pass the Daoyi Gate, the Gate of Innate Heaven, the Gate of the Great Ultimate, the Hall of Unifying Heaven, and the Hall of Manifest Benevolence, until you reach the burial mound of Taihao Fuxi — a massive circular tumulus about twenty-five meters high and over one hundred and eighty meters in circumference, covered in verdant ancient cypresses, solemn and mysterious. The Hall of Unifying Heaven is the temple's core, bearing an inscription of four large characters: "人根之祖" (Progenitor of the Human Race). Here Fuxi is not an illusory mythic symbol but a "real" presence worshipped as an ancestor by generation after generation. Amid swirling incense smoke, elderly women prostrate themselves in kowtow, children gaze with curious eyes — in this mortal atmosphere of smoke and fire, Fuxi becomes almost tangible. Interestingly, Fuxi does not appear directly in The Investiture of the Gods, but the novel's concept of "Heaven's mandate" is deeply rooted in the cosmic order initiated by Fuxi's drawing of the Eight Trigrams. The list Jiang Ziya recited on the Investiture Terrace — Huang Feihu, the Saintly Emperor of the Eastern Peak Mount Tai; Chong Heihu, the Saintly Emperor of the Southern Peak Mount Heng... — was in fact a redistribution of divine authority on the foundation of a far more ancient belief system. And the source of that belief system was the eight trigrams Fuxi drew by observing the patterns of heaven above and the forms of earth below. From eight trigrams to sixty-four hexagrams, from sixty-four hexagrams to the three hundred and sixty-five principal deities on the Investiture Rolls, the Chinese understanding of the relationship between heaven, earth, and humanity has traveled a long and profound road. Every year from the second day of the second lunar month to the third day of the third, the Taihao Mausoleum temple fair draws hundreds of thousands of worshippers — the vitality of the Fuxi myth is more powerful than any novel. At dusk, standing on the high platform before the Hall of Unifying Heaven and looking south, the ten-thousand-mu Dragon Lake shimmers. Legend says that Fuxi taught the people here to weave nets and fish, opening the first page of the Chinese people's transition from hunting and gathering to farming. The blue smoke of the tower incense turns gold in the sunset; bells sound from afar. Investiture, investiture — the gods are not names sealed on a roll; they are sealed in the human heart. Every wisp of incense at the Taihao Mausoleum is this people's eternal questioning of "beginning" and "end."

stops.title: Stop Four: White Horse Temple in Luoyang · After the Conflict, a Return to Compassion
stops.content: The Shang gave way to Zhou, the Investiture ended, and peace returned to the realm. But the horrific battles in the novel — the Immortals-Slaying Formation, the Ten Thousand Immortals Formation, the Yellow River Formation — with countless immortals falling and endless suffering, make one ask: amid the rise and fall of dynasties, is there a compassion that transcends killing? Centuries later, Buddhism entered China from the Western Regions, and the first officially established temple was built outside Luoyang. The White Horse Temple is the first temple built after Buddhism entered China. The story of "the white horse carrying the sutras" has been told for nearly two thousand years. Within the temple, ancient cypresses tower, incense smoke curls, and the cool sound of the bell soothes countless souls that once struggled on the battlefields of the Investiture. From the flashing blades of the Investiture Rolls to the morning bells and evening drums of the White Horse Temple — the depth of Chinese culture lies precisely in its ability, after the clash of gold and iron, to give the human heart a place to rest in compassion. The White Horse Temple was first built in the eleventh year of Yongping, Eastern Han (68 AD), nearly two thousand years ago. Two stone horses before the temple gate — one left, one right, heads lowered as if bearing a burden — silently tell the story of the Indian monks Kasyapa Matanga and Dharmaratna bringing the sutras eastward on white horses. Entering the mountain gate, the Heavenly King Hall, Great Buddha Hall, Great Shakyamuni Hall, Welding Hall, and Vairocana Pavilion ascend in layers along the central axis. The Buddhas of the Three Ages in the Great Shakyamuni Hall — Shakyamuni, Bhaisajyaguru, and Amitabha — were made using the Yuan-dynasty dry-lacquer technique, light as wood yet hard as stone, unbroken for a thousand years. Morning light slants through the latticework of the hall's doors, falling on the compassionate curve of the Buddha's lips; the air is thick with sandalwood and the scent of ancient timber. Close your eyes, and you can hear the wind chimes at the corner of the hall — the sound neither hurried nor slow. Three-thousand-year-old battles, two-thousand-year-old camel bells, a thousand-year-old wooden fish — all are blended into this wind. The temple also houses the Qiyun Pagoda, built in the Jin dynasty — a thirteen-story, twenty-five-meter dense-eave brick pagoda that leans slightly eastward. The pagoda bells ring in the wind, as if telling an ancient secret. The fallen immortals of The Investiture of the Gods — Zhao Gongming, the Three Skylark Ladies, Golden Spirit Mother — if they could sit beneath the White Horse Temple's ancient cypresses and listen to this bell, they too might lay down their obsessions. Less than three li east lies the Han-Wei Luoyang Ancient City (including the Biyong Stele) — the capital site of the Eastern Han, Cao Wei, Western Jin, and Northern Wei, with city wall fragments about fourteen kilometers in circumference visible among the fields. This was the first stop of Buddhism's eastward transmission, the site where "the quest for the Dharma in Yongping" occurred — the story of Chinese Buddhism began in this land of Luoyang. One temple, one city — two millennia converge here. The "invested" gods on the Investiture Rolls and the "enshrined" Buddhas in the temple hall together form the richest foundation of the Chinese spiritual world.

buildings.n: Luoyang Ancient City of Han and Wei Dynasties

stops.title: Stop Five: The Banks of the Wei River · Jiang the Grand Duke Fishes
stops.content: The most captivating scene in The Investiture of the Gods is surely Jiang Ziya fishing on the banks of the Wei River — "Better to take on a straight hook than to beg on a bent one." An eighty-year-old white-haired old man, fishing with a straight hook — not for carp, but for a prince. King Wen of Zhou, seeking worthy men, personally pulled the old man's carriage for eight hundred paces, and the Grand Duke promised the Zhou dynasty eight hundred years of rule. This highly ritualized encounter is the very beginning of the entire Investiture epic. The Wei River flows eastward through Baoji. The Zhou Plains Site in the upper reaches and the banks of the Wei together form the panoramic setting of "Jiang the Grand Duke fishes." Though the exact location of the fishing terrace is hard to verify, standing on the banks of this river that witnessed Chinese civilization's journey from obscurity to rites and music, feeling the same wind that has blown for millennia, you understand an eighty-year-old man's unruffled calm — he knew he was not waiting for a fish, but for an era. In the Fayu River Valley fifteen kilometers southeast of Baoji, there is a scenic spot called "Jiang Ziya's Fishing Terrace" — the river turns here to form a deep pool, and on the bank a huge slab of blue stone lies flat like a platform. Two deep knee-prints on the stone are said to be left by the Grand Duke as he fished. The pool is deep and green, the mountain shadow reflected on its surface; occasionally an egret skims over the water, startling a circle of ripples. The Records of the Grand Historian records this legendary meeting: "Lü Shang was once down on his luck, old now, and fished to gain an audience with the Western Earl. The Western Earl was about to go hunting and cast a divination. The oracle said: 'What you catch will be no dragon or monster, no tiger or bear; what you catch will be an adviser for a hegemonic king.' So the Western Earl went hunting and indeed met the Grand Duke on the north bank of the Wei." King Wen was overjoyed and said: "My Grand Duke has long been waiting for you!" — and thus "Grand Duke Wang" became Jiang Ziya's name. Drive west along the Wei River for less than a hundred li and you reach the Duke of Zhou Temple. After the successful campaign against Zhou, the Grand Duke was enfeoffed in Qi, while the Duke of Zhou was enfeoffed in Lu. One represented "martial achievement," the other "civil governance" — just as the Wei has two banks, Chinese civilization also advanced through two complementary forces. Standing on the banks of the Wei, the river flows broad and strong. No bait, no float needed. What Jiang Ziya "angled" for was not fish, but the Zhou dynasty's eight hundred years under heaven. And the real "fish" — the Zhou dynasty that struck from the banks of the Wei into Zhaoge — has long since become The Investiture of the Gods, alive and leaping in every person's heart. The Wei River has flowed eastward in silence for three thousand years. The Grand Duke's straight hook still waits for the next one to pull the carriage.

stops.title: Stop Six: Weihui · Bi Gan's Ripped-Out Heart — Loyalty for a Thousand Autumns
stops.content:
The death of Bi Gan is one of the most heart-wrenching episodes in The Investiture of the Gods. King Zhou trusted the enchanting Daji, abandoned himself to debauchery, and ignored all counsel. Bi Gan remonstrated at the cost of his life and had his heart ripped out. The novel writes that after his heart was cut out, Bi Gan rode his horse out of the city. By the roadside he met a woman selling heartless vegetables. He asked her: "A vegetable can live without a heart, but how can a man live without one?" Bi Gan could not answer and fell dead from his horse. This tragic and absurd passage reveals a brutal truth: before tyranny, the heart of a loyal minister is the sacrificial offering.

The Bi Gan Temple in Weihui, Henan, is China's first memorial complex combining a temple and a tomb. First built in the Northern Wei dynasty, it is now over 1,500 years old. Within the temple, ancient cypresses are thick and stelae stand in rows. When Confucius traveled through this land, he wrote the four characters "殷比干墓" (Tomb of Bi Gan of Yin) which were erected before the tomb — this is the sole surviving calligraphic relic of Confucius. The main structures of the temple — the screen wall, mountain gate, second gate, wooden archway, stele corridor, worshipping hall, main hall, stone archway, and tomb mound — ascend in layers, solemn and majestic. The statue of Bi Gan sits upright in the main hall, holding his official tablet, his gaze firm without a trace of fear or regret — only the calm of one who has discerned Heaven's mandate.

In the temple stands a "heartless cypress" — hollow at the core yet still lush and vigorous, said to symbolize Bi Gan's spirit. In the courtyard is also a "heart-opening well" — its water sweet, reputedly where Bi Gan washed his heart after it was torn out. Every year on the fourth day of the fourth lunar month, Bi Gan's birthday, descendants of the Lin clan from home and abroad gather before the temple — Bi Gan is honored as the "Supreme Ancestor of the Lin Clan." The stele corridor before the temple is engraved with the names of Lin family notables through the ages: Lin Zexu, Lin Huiyin... The spirit of loyalty has passed through bloodlines for generation after generation. Driving northeast from the Bi Gan Temple, within less than a hundred li, you reach the land of Zhaoge — the Yinxu ruins of Anyang. The place where King Zhou committed his evils and the place where Bi Gan died for his loyalty are barely a stone's throw apart in space and time, yet the distance between good and evil, loyalty and treachery spans a chasm of three thousand years.
